How the Context Layer, Corpus & RAG actually work

A plain-English, full-stack walk-through: what data lives in the context layer, how documents become searchable chunks, how Sentinel and Nexus become "context-aware" in real time, what happens when there is no context (and Claude answers from its own memory), the role of the reasoning layer — and how we make these agents answer better over time. Grounded in the live lab data plane.

00 · Start here

TL;DR for a layman

The 30-second version. AbarVa keeps a private "memory" for each client (the context layer) plus a shared library of reusable "what works / what fails" lessons (the corpus / patterns). When you ask Sentinel or Nexus a question, the system first retrieves the most relevant pieces of that memory, pastes them into the question, and only then asks Claude (the large language model) to write the answer — so the answer is grounded in your real data with citations. This technique is called RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). If there is no relevant context, Claude still answers from its own general training, but the system marks it as lower-confidence and the reasoning layer adds guardrails (e.g., "don't claim a number you can't cite").

Four moving parts to remember: 1 · Ingestion (files → chunks) 2 · Stores (DB + graph + vector + blob) 3 · Retrieval & binding (context broker) 4 · Generation (Claude) + reasoning guardrails

01 · The client's private memory

What's in the context layer, by dimension

The context layer is per-client (tenant-scoped). Every row carries a tenant_key (e.g. lakeshore-holdings) and a client_id, so one client can never see another's data. The main table is enterprise_context_chunks in Azure Postgres abarva_control.

02 · The shared library of lessons

Corpus & patterns inventory

Separate from any one client's data, AbarVa keeps a shared library of reusable patterns — codified "what works / what fails, with failure rates and controls." Sentinel uses these to reason like an experienced operator, not just summarize your documents.

Two namespaces, don't confuse them. A client's private memory (enterprise_context_chunks / tenant-context-v1) is different from the shared lessons (genome_patterns / corpus_patterns). The treasury pattern LSH-TMS-002 lives in the genome registry; a generic corpus slug like PAT-LSH-D18-00479 lives in corpus_patterns. Binding the wrong namespace to a card is the class of bug the "fail-closed pattern grounding" fix addresses.
03 · Ingestion

How a file becomes searchable: chunk → registry → DB → graph → vector → index

Plain English: a PDF/Excel/Word file is read, its text is pulled out, sliced into bite-sized "chunks," each chunk is saved as a database row, turned into a list of numbers (an "embedding") that captures its meaning, and copied into a search index so it can be found by meaning, not just keywords.
Figure 1 — Ingestion pipeline. One file fans out to four stores (DB row, graph, evidence) and two search/vector copies.
StepWhat happensReal component
1 UploadZIP/files via Setup Admin/api/admin/context-layer/bulk-upload
2 BlobOriginal bytes kept for evidenceobjectStorage.ts → context-drops
3 ParseExtract text from pdf/docx/xlsx/pptxparseIngestionDocument()
4 ChunkSlice into rows (1/CSV row; ~1.2k chars/doc)csv-upload-connector / worker
5 CommitRows → Postgres; facts → graph; claims → ledgerenterprise_context_chunks, enterprise_graph_*, evidence_ledger
6 EmbedEach chunk → 1536-number "meaning vector"OpenAI text-embedding-3-small
7 IndexCopy text+vector into searchAzure AI Search tenant-context-v1
04 · The four homes of context

Where context is stored (and why four places)

① Azure Blob — the originals

The untouched source files (the PDF/Excel) so any claim can be traced to the exact document. stabarvaprivatedplab001/context-drops/<tenant>/…

② Azure Postgres — the chunk registry

The system of record: enterprise_context_chunks (text + 1536-d vector + provenance), plus data_ingestion_runs (audit). This is the "truth."

③ Graph — the relationships

enterprise_graph_nodes/edges connect facts (e.g., "Kyriba → bank → payment file"), so reasoning can follow links, not just match text.

④ Azure AI Search — the fast finder

tenant-context-v1 holds a searchable copy (keyword BM25 + vector) so retrieval at question-time is milliseconds. Postgres is truth; Search is speed.

Why not one store? Postgres is reliable and exact but slow for "find me the 8 most similar paragraphs." Search/vector is fast for similarity. Graph captures relationships. Blob keeps the legal original. Each is best at one job; the broker stitches them together.
05 · The magic moment

Real-time binding: how Sentinel & Nexus become "context-aware"

Plain English: When you ask a question, a component called the Context Broker runs a search across your private memory (and the shared patterns), picks the most relevant pieces, and pastes them into a hidden "here's what you know" block in front of your question. Claude then answers using that block. The agent isn't "trained on" your data — it's handed the right data, fresh, every single time.
Figure 2 — Real-time binding. The broker retrieves, assembles a context block, and Claude generates a grounded, cited answer — per request, no model retraining.
06 · "Who holds the intelligence?"

Which component is configured to know about context

There isn't one "brain" — the awareness is split across a few well-defined components. This is the part most people get wrong: the LLM (Claude) is stateless; it knows nothing about your data until the broker hands it over. The "knowing where to look" lives in code + configuration:

ConcernComponent (the "config" that knows)File
Which tenant am I?Tenant resolver (email/cookie/Clerk → client_id, tenant_key)resolveTenant.ts, active-client.ts
Which stores to query & howContext Brokerknowledge/agent-context-broker.ts
Vector vs keyword, on/off per tenantFeature flag registryfeatures/registry.ts (retrieval_azure_search)
Where the context livesData-plane adaptersdata-plane/azureRead.ts, azure-search/*
What to inject into the promptTenant context block builder + phase packsintelligence/persistence.ts (buildTenantContextBlock)
Sentinel "voice" & grounding rulesVoice doctrine + Ask orchestratoragent/voice-doctrine/sentinel.ts, intelligence/ask/index.ts
Nexus per-phase awarenessNexus context assembler + phase packsprograms/nexus.ts, programs-broker-adapter.ts
Guardrails (no uncited claims)Failure-mode prompt + guardrail modelprograms/failure-mode-prompt.ts, agent/guardrail.ts
Plain English: Sentinel and Nexus are the same engine pointed at different jobs. Sentinel = "ask the intelligence anything" (merges your facts + shared patterns + worldview). Nexus = "guide me through building a Move" (adds the current phase's playbook). Both get their awareness from the broker + config, not from any baked-in memory.
07 · End to end

Worked example: "Evaluate the Kyriba global treasury rollout"

#What happensConcretely
1You ask Sentinel on the Lakeshore tenanttenant_key = lakeshore-holdings
2Broker retrieves private contextSearch tenant-context-v1 filter tenant_key eq 'lakeshore-holdings' → top treasury chunks (rollout plan, bank connectivity, defects)
3Broker retrieves shared lessonsgenome_patterns treasury → LSH-TMS-002 "Bank connectivity matrix clears before rollout"
4Assemble context block + guardrailstop chunks + pattern + "cite or don't claim" rule
5Claude generatesgrounded answer: cash visibility, exception rate, controls — each tied to a source
6Answer returned with citationslinks back to blob docs + pattern id
The grounding bug we fixed (live example). A treasury decision card had bound PAT-LSH-D18-00479 — a real corpus slug, but a procurement pattern, not treasury. That's a cross-namespace mis-binding. The fix makes the binder fail closed: a treasury card binds only the treasury namespace (LSH-TMS-*) or nothing — never an off-topic pattern. This is the difference between an answer that "sounds right" and one that's grounded right.
08 · When the cupboard is bare

No context? How we still answer (the Claude-only path)

Plain English: If the broker finds nothing relevant in your memory, Claude answers from its own general training (what it learned from the public internet up to its cutoff). That's still useful — but it is generic, not about your company, and it can be out of date or wrong on specifics. So the system marks it lower-confidence and the reasoning layer forbids inventing precise numbers.
Figure 3 — The fallback. With context → grounded RAG answer. Without → Claude's general knowledge, gated by the reasoning layer and labeled as generic.
DimensionWith context (RAG)Without context (Claude-only)
SourceYour documents + shared patternsClaude's training data
Specific numbersYes, cited to a fileAvoided (guardrail blocks fake precision)
Confidence labelHigh, with evidence"General guidance"
RiskLow (grounded)Hallucination if unguarded
09 · The thinking in between

The reasoning layer — what it adds beyond "retrieve then generate"

RAG alone is "find text, summarize text." The reasoning layer makes the answer behave like an expert: it checks for contradictions, surfaces known failure modes, evaluates gates, and refuses ungrounded claims.

What it does

  • Contradiction detection — flags when retrieved facts disagree.
  • Failure-mode injection — adds the canonical 10 ways these programs fail.
  • Gate evaluation — is this Move ready to advance a phase?
  • Grounding guard — every claim must map to evidence (or be dropped).
  • Honesty — payback = null when monetization is blocked; "shape" not "fund."

Where it lives

  • reasoning/program-synthesis-context-builder.ts
  • programs/failure-mode-prompt.ts
  • expert-kernel/critic.ts (CFO/delivery/data lenses)
  • expert-kernel/qa-rubric.ts + artifact quality rubric
  • intelligence-v3/pattern-grounding.ts (namespace fail-closed)
Analogy: RAG is the junior analyst who fetches the right files. The reasoning layer is the partner who asks "does this contradict itself? what usually goes wrong here? can you prove this number?" before the answer leaves the room.
10 · Getting better over time

How to "train" Sentinel & Nexus to answer better

Key insight: for this system, "training" mostly does not mean fine-tuning the LLM. Claude is fixed; you improve answers by improving what you feed it and how you check it. Fine-tuning is the last lever, not the first.
Figure 4 — The improvement loop. Six levers, run continuously; fine-tuning the LLM is optional and last.
LeverWhat you changeConcrete actions (this codebase)
1 · Corpus qualityMake the retrieved knowledge deeper/cleanerRun depth-lint rubrics; enforce OWN-IT + anti-patterns + evidence anchors; author missing domain packs (e.g., a true corporate-treasury pack); de-duplicate.
2 · Retrieval qualityFind the right chunks, not just similar textTurn on hybrid (vector + BM25) + a reranker; tune top-k & thresholds; grounding-namespace validation so off-topic patterns can't bind; add query expansion.
3 · Prompt / doctrineHow the agent is told to reasonImprove voice-doctrine + failure-mode-prompt; require citations; few-shot exemplars of great answers.
4 · EvaluationsMeasure answer quality automaticallyGrow the eval set (eval/answer-quality, pass ≥75; cxo-answer-quality); add Q&A pairs per dimension; track regressions in CI.
5 · Human-in-loopCalibrate to expert judgmentExpert-review console (CFO + partner sign-off); capture thumbs-up/down + corrections as labeled data.
6 · Feedback loopClose the loop continuouslyLog every retrieval + answer; mine failures; feed corrections back into corpus/evals; re-run.
7 · Fine-tune (last)Change the model's defaultsOnly if 1–6 plateau: fine-tune/distill a smaller model for style/format, never as a substitute for grounding. RAG still supplies the facts.
Rule of thumb: 80% of "make it smarter" is levers 1–4 (corpus + retrieval + prompt + evals). If Sentinel gives a weak answer, the first question is almost always "did it retrieve the right context?" — not "is the model dumb?" The grounding fix in this very project is a textbook lever-2 improvement.
11 · Plain definitions

Glossary

TermIn one sentence
LLM (Claude)A large language model that writes text; it has no memory of your data unless you give it.
RAGRetrieval-Augmented Generation — fetch relevant facts first, then let the LLM write using them.
Context layerA client's private, searchable memory built from their uploaded documents.
ChunkA bite-sized piece of a document (a row) that can be searched and cited.
Embedding / vectorA list of numbers capturing a chunk's meaning, so "similar meaning" = "close numbers."
Corpus / patternsShared, reusable lessons ("what works/fails") across clients and industries.
Context BrokerThe component that decides what to retrieve and assembles it for the LLM.
SentinelThe "ask anything" advisor agent (intelligence Q&A, grounded + worldview).
NexusThe guided agent that helps build a Strategic Move phase by phase.
Reasoning layerThe logic that checks contradictions, failure modes, gates, and enforces grounding.
Grounding / namespaceMaking sure a cited pattern actually belongs to the topic (treasury vs procurement).
BM25 vs vectorKeyword match vs meaning match; "hybrid" uses both for best recall.
